hook.text: Every token a model reads, writes or thinks ends up on a bill.

kinds.text: Your prompt is what it reads. The answer is what it writes. And a reasoning model's thinking is written too, even though you never see it.

ask.text: So what does a token actually cost?

sheet.text: Every big provider prices tokens the same way: five prices per million tokens, always in the same proportions.

rows.text: Input is the baseline. Output, five times that or more. Cached input, a tenth or less. Writing to the cache, a little over input. And batch, about half off.

ratios.text: The prices keep falling. The ratios hardly move.

why.text: So why does output cost so much more? It's not a pricing whim. It's the computation.

parallel.text: Your prompt goes through the model all at once, in one parallel pass.

serial.text: The answer comes out one token at a time, and every token needs its own pass through the whole model.

gap.text: Five times the price is a real gap in the work.

cached.text: Cached input runs the other way.

reuse.text: Send the same fifty-thousand-token prefix every turn, and the provider can keep what it computed and just read it back.

twentieth.text: That's about a tenth of the work, and some models now charge a twentieth. On Sonnet, ten cents a turn becomes half a cent.

prefix.text: The catch: it only matches an exact prefix. Put a timestamp at the top, and one changed byte sends everything after it back to full price.

market.text: Here's the market in October twenty twenty-six.

ratio.text: Output is five times input in eight of these ten rows, and never less.

spread.text: But the cheapest input, ten cents a million, is a hundredth of the priciest, ten dollars.

choice.text: So the model you pick usually moves the bill more than any prompt trick.

threshold.text: And half these rows hide a length threshold. Past two hundred seventy-two thousand tokens on GPT six, the whole request pays double for its input.

oversized.text: So on Sol, a three-hundred-thousand-token prompt costs a dollar twenty to send, not sixty cents.

estimate-in.text: That's the price sheet. Now, what does a real workload cost?

request.text: Take one support-bot request: twelve hundred tokens in, three hundred out.

nothing.text: On Sonnet, that's about half a cent. Basically nothing.

volume.text: Now serve a hundred thousand of them. Twenty-seven dollars on Haiku, twenty-seven hundred on Fable.

apart.text: Same task, same tokens, a hundred times apart.

resend.text: Conversations are where estimates go wrong.

stateless.text: The model keeps no memory between turns, so every turn resends the whole chat so far.

slice.text: The new message is a thin slice on top of everything you've already paid for.

turns.text: On Sonnet, ten turns cost thirteen cents. Twenty, thirty-seven and a half. Forty, a dollar nineteen.

triple.text: Double the turns, and the bill roughly triples, and it keeps getting worse.

think.text: Thinking tokens are the other surprise. They're billed as output.

budget.text: Keep the request and its four-hundred-token answer the same. Add eight thousand thinking tokens, and it costs eleven times as much. Twenty thousand, twenty-six times.

invisible.text: And the answer you see never got any longer.

month.text: Now put a whole month together: four workloads, each with its own model and volume.

guess.text: Code review on Opus looks like the big line. [curious] It isn't.

answer.text: Document summaries on Sonnet are, at eight hundred sixty-four dollars a month, because volume and tokens multiply.

total.text: The whole month comes to about seventeen hundred and sixty dollars.

control-in.text: So once you can see the bill, how do you shrink it?

levers.text: Six levers, in the order they usually pay off.

route.text: First, route each task to the cheapest model that passes.

route-cost.text: Fifty thousand classifications a day cost four thousand and fifty dollars a month on Opus, and a hundred and one on Haiku.

cache.text: Second, cache the stable prefix: whatever never changes goes first. That forty-turn chat drops from a dollar nineteen to twenty-six cents.

output.text: Third, cut output, not input. Each output token you save is worth five input ones.

effort.text: Fourth, turn reasoning effort, the thinking budget, down to the lowest level that passes.

batch.text: Fifth, batch anything nobody's waiting on, at about half off.

prompt.text: And only then, trim the prompt.

passes.text: Notice the word that came up twice: passes.

next.text: Passes what? That takes a test, and that's next: measuring whether a model is good enough.

weights.text: Each pass moves every weight in the model, whether it carries eleven tokens or one. So while it writes, the hardware mostly waits.

sum.text: The bill pays for every one of these bars, plus each reply.

cache-resend.text: You still resend it all. The provider just recognizes that part and reads it back.
